On Wednesday, January 26, 2022 at 7:06:01 AM UTC+8 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I want to see if age, an observed variable can predict the differences in attitude towards blue and red
>
> The means of the blue and red factors are only comparable if their scales are linked.  Assuming their indicators are parallel (so first indicator of blue is essentially the same as the first indicator of red), then you can test measurement invariance across the constructs.  This is the same method used when measuring the same construct on multiple occasions (longitudinal invariance), but it can apply to any dependent/repeated measures (e.g., mother and father factors for responses about the same child).
>
> If scalar ("strong") invariance holds, then you can identify the model by fixing the first factor (e.g., blue) mean to zero but freely estimate the other factor (e.g., red) mean.  Thus, the red mean would already be the mean difference between blue and red.  And you can use age as a predictor of red to obtain any moderating effect on the red mean (and thus the mean difference you are interested in).  Even though the blue mean is fixed to zero, you can estimate the age effect on that too.  In this case, to make sure the red mean remains the marginal mean difference between factors, you should mean-center age.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I know it is not addressed to me, but I guess trying to help is not the worst thing one can do. level : 2

I think you can try to run the multilevel analysis without specifying the regressions (if that is your goal). In that case you would perform a multilevel CFA instead of a multilevel SEM analysis. I am not an expert on this matter, so confirmation from someone else would be great!

messages.subject: Re: Separating shared/specific/residual variances with known reliability
messages.subject_clean: Separating shared/specific/residual variances with known reliability
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Terrance and Wen! This is very helpful.

On Friday, January 28, 2022 at 11:32:28 AM UTC Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I can estimate the reliability of each indicator in a preceding stage
>
> Reliable variance is just systematically repeatable components.  In the preceding stage, any shared variance that is in common among all the indicators will be considered part of the "true score" in classical test theory.  Their variance is reliable.
>
> If that holds across all 3 indicators at their preceding stages, then their reliable specific-error variance is retained in the composite, along with the construct variance of interest, rather than being proportionally minimized as indicator-specific measurement error is (even if that includes reliable specific variance unique that indicator).
>
> So at the current stage, the same applies.  Any specific variance that is in common across the 3 composite indicators (whose reliabilities you estimated previously) will be confounded with the construct variance of interest.  Any specific variance that is unique to a composite will be confounded with that composite's other unique sources of (systematic and random) measurement error.
>
> > I would assume
>
> Incorrectly (sorry), unless you have 3 separate estimates of the construct, specific-error, and random-error variances in each composite.
>
> > What is the core difference between having separate sub-indicators of an indicator (allowing to estimate measurement error), and specifying the measurement error manually in this case?
>
> The difference is whether you have unique information about each source of variance to facilitate decomposing them in a model.  Hopefully you have access to this article to read: https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000107
> Vispoel et al. (2018) provide a great discussion of reliability/generalizability in CTT, (C)FA, and GT.  Pay close attention to their interpretation of a one-facet design (e.g., multiple occasions to quantify test-retest reliability), in which random measurement error is confounded with any other source of systematic variance that was not part of the design (e.g., multiple items or raters).  A two-facet design can be used to decompose systematic error associated with both occasions and raters from random measurement error, the latter of which remains confounded with the occasion-rater interaction as well as any other systematic error not part of the design (e.g., multiple scale items or tasks).
>
> It sounds like you have data that conform to a hierarchical CFA (lower-order factors indicate a higher-order factor), but are using composites as the indicators of the higher-order factor.  Perhaps you can model them altogether, and use semTools::reliabilityL2() to calculated reliability of the higher-order construct.
> Or you could conceive of the 3 composite indicators as 3 different measurement conditions, in each of which are nested different scale times.  That would give you a 2 (nested) facet GT design, or maybe a 2 crossed facet design if the scale items are conceptually parallel across the 3 composite indicators.  Then you could use a CFA of GT.  I provide lavaan examples for my open-access tutorial:
> https://osf.io/43j5x/
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Re: Residual covariances in moderated mediation with latent variables (indProd)
messages.subject_clean: Residual covariances in moderated mediation with latent variables (indProd)
messages.body_plain:
The product terms become the indicators of the interaction factor, so change the ~~ to =~ in your first line:

latent_interaction =~ item_A1.itemB1 + item_A1.itemB2 + item_A1.itemB3 + item_A1.itemB4 + item_A1.itemB5 + item_A2.itemB1 ... etc

(You said that A had 5 items and B had 3 items, but this line of syntax suggests the other way around.)
Then the rule for residual covariances, in the absence of matching, is to allow a residual covariance for every pair of product indicators that share a term. So, for example, your next line of code:

item_A1.itemB1 ~~ item_A1.itemB2 + item_A1.itemB3 + item_A1.itemB4 + item_A1.itemB5

does the job for product terms containing item_A1.
If A has 3 items, then you will need 2 more lines like this, one for A2 and one for A3.

That should specify the 15 residual covariances (3 x 5) that the no-matching strategy entails.

--Ed Rigdon

Yes, that's the correct set of covariances for the A items, you also need to include residual covariances for the B items (e.g. all items with B1 covary). >
> "

>
> "

>
>

>
> )
>

>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> # x.boot custom function
>

>

>

>
>   }, object)
>
> }
>

>

messages.subject: Re: Question about identified model
messages.body_plain:
Yes, the structural model that you describe is fundamentally not identified. Each structural variable (your F, E and P) needs its own predictor not shared with the other structural variables. The observed variable indicators (F1, F2 and so forth) do not count. There is no way to resolve this without the additional predictors.
You can see the problem by looking at the covariance matrix of the structural variables:
     F   P   E
F   x
P   x    x
E   x    x   x
Currently, you are trying to estimate 6 structural paths from the 6 unique elements of this covariance matrix, but you also have to estimate 3 residual variances for the 3 structural variables. That is estimating 9 unknowns from the 6 knowns--if we treat this covariance matrix itself as known. The algebra for obtaining unique solutions for model parameters will not work without additional predictors for F, P and E.
--Ed Rigdon

Dear All,
I would appreciate it if you helped me regarding the following topic. Your answers will help me a lot in solving an issue in my thesis.

I used Lavaan for doing the following autoregressive cross-lagged model. the data for Esdq is available from 3years to 17 years old children at baseline with an index of 0
Esdq1: 6 -17 years age rangeEsdq2: 11-17 years age rangePA0:  0-17 yearsPA1: 6-17 years PA2:11-17 years
I want to find out how lavaan (R) uses the data for cross-lagged paths. Does it only use paired data from the previous time-point to the next time-point ? or does it use the data from the previous time-point that there is no pair data for it at the next time-point. In other words: does lavaan use only data of participants that they have valid data at two-time points in terms of cross-lagged paths or not?
ReciprocalcovModel3 <-
  '
  Esdq2 ~ Esdq1+Esdq0+ PA1+Bmi2
  Esdq1 ~ Esdq0+ PA0+Ebmi1
  PA2 ~ PA1+ PA0+Esdq1+Bmi2
  PA1 ~ PA0+Esdq0+Ebmi1
  Esdq0~UBmi0+SESc0
  PA0~UBmi0+SESc0
  Esdq0 ~~ PA0
  Esdq1 ~~ PA1
  Esdq2 ~~ PA2

 '

Parisa

messages.body_plain:
If you have too few data points for multilevel models at the class level, you have too few data points to estimate clustered (sandwich /robust / Huber-White) standard errors.

The common solutions to this, are either to include class as a fixed effect in the model, or to do something Bayesian, where a prior can help with the problems you get with uncertainty at the higher level.

Perhaps tell us more about your data?

Jeremy

Hi all,

I had a question about moderation in longitudinal data and am wondering if lavaan would be an appropriate package to use in my analysis; I see much about multilevel mediation, but not moderation.

I am analyzing a dataset of psychotherapy clients, and am looking to examine how reduction in symptoms between sessions is predicted by client-level factors that vary at the session level. I am particularly interested in if there is a moderation effect of a client-factor (perceptions of secrecy in session) on the therapist & client relationship, such that its predictive effect (better relationship, more symptom change) is attenuated by client secrecy. I also have several covariates (e.g., ratings of session "goodness").

I am trying to read the literature but what I am finding is mostly about moderation using a time-invariant predictor. I am not necessarily interested in detecting between & within-person differences, but simply harnessing the repeated measures to provide a more robust test of a possible moderation factor across psychotherapy sessions.

I was wondering if anyone can point me in a good direction regarding how to approach handling data like this in lavaan. Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running some longitudinal CFAs to see whether they are invariant across time (three time points from the same individuals). I am manually constraining the loadings and intercepts to be equal. Example:

cfa.emot.inter <- "
emotional_problems1 =~ sdq_1*SDQ_1_E + sdq_2*SDQ_4_E + sdq_3*SDQ_6_E + sdq_4*SDQ_7_E + sdq_5*SDQ_10_E

emotional_problems2 =~ sdq_1*T2_SDQ_1_E + sdq_2*T2_SDQ_4_E + sdq_3*T2_SDQ_6_E + sdq_4*T2_SDQ_7_E + sdq_5*T2_SDQ_10_E

emotional_problems3 =~ sdq_1*T3_SDQ_1_E + sdq_2*T3_SDQ_4_E + sdq_3*T3_SDQ_6_E + sdq_4*T3_SDQ_7_E + sdq_5*T3_SDQ_10_E

emotional_problems1 ~~ emotional_problems2
emotional_problems1 ~~ emotional_problems3
emotional_problems2 ~~ emotional_problems3

# Intercepts

SDQ_1_E ~ sdq_i1*1
SDQ_4_E ~ sdq_i2*1
SDQ_6_E ~ sdq_i3*1
SDQ_7_E ~ sdq_i4*1
SDQ_10_E ~ sdq_i5*1

T2_SDQ_1_E ~ sdq_i1*1
T2_SDQ_4_E ~ sdq_i2*1
T2_SDQ_6_E ~ sdq_i3*1
T2_SDQ_7_E ~ sdq_i4*1
T2_SDQ_10_E ~ sdq_i5*1

T3_SDQ_1_E ~ sdq_i1*1
T3_SDQ_4_E ~ sdq_i2*1
T3_SDQ_6_E ~ sdq_i3*1
T3_SDQ_7_E ~ sdq_i4*1
T3_SDQ_10_E ~ sdq_i5*1

I found that the scalar model shows a worse fit according to ∆CFI = .051. If we go off conventional standards then ∆CFI should not be over .01. I tried to use the lavTestScore() to see which parameter is causing the issue. The problem is since I have manually constrained my loadings and intercepts, I can't tell which parameter the function is referring to. Perhaps there is a better approach?

I am trying to assess the longitudinal invariance prior to running a random-intercepts cross-lagged panel model with three latent variables, so maybe another question is, how important would scalar invariance be?

Best,
Emily

Hello,

Below, I have my model adapted from (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187892931730021X). I am struggling to understand how I can include a group level in this model.

Specifically, I would like to split the model by 'Age_group' which has a factor of "older' and 'younger' adults. I know I need to use something like c(x,y) but I am not sure where in the model to insert it. Any help is appreciated.

BDCS<-'

COGlv_T1=~1*RAVLT_DELAY_bl         # Defining the COG latent variables
COGlv_T2=~1*RAVLT_DELAY_flu1       # Defining the COG latent variables
COGlv_T3=~1*RAVLT_DELAY_flu2       # Defining the COG latent variables

NEUlv_T1=~1*mean_AD_bl           # Defining the NEU latent variables
NEUlv_T2=~1*mean_AD_flu1         # Defining the NEU latent variables
NEUlv_T3=~1*mean_AD_flu2         # Defining the NEU latent variables

##### The following parameters capture the core assumptions of the LCS and should not generally be modified

COGlv_T2 ~ 1*COGlv_T1     # This parameter regresses COG_T2 perfectly on COG_T1
COGlv_T3 ~ 1*COGlv_T2     # This parameter regresses COG_T3 perfectly on COG_T2

NEUlv_T2 ~ 1*NEUlv_T1     # This parameter regresses NEU_T2 perfectly on NEU_T1
NEUlv_T3 ~ 1*NEUlv_T2     # This parameter regresses NEU_T3 perfectly on NEU_T2

dRAVLT_DELAY_bl   =~ 1*COGlv_T2       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on COG_T2
dRAVLT_DELAY_flu1 =~ 1*COGlv_T3       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on COG_T3

dmean_AD_bl   =~ 1*NEUlv_T2       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on NEU_T2
dmean_AD_flu1 =~ 1*NEUlv_T3       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on NEU_T3

RAVLT_DELAY_bl   ~~resCOGvar*RAVLT_DELAY_bl          # This estimates the COG residual variances
RAVLT_DELAY_flu1 ~~resCOGvar*RAVLT_DELAY_flu1        # This estimates the COG residual variances
RAVLT_DELAY_flu2 ~~resCOGvar*RAVLT_DELAY_flu2        # This estimates the COG residual variances

mean_AD_bl   ~~resNEUvar*mean_AD_bl              # This estimates the NEU residual variances
mean_AD_flu1 ~~resNEUvar*mean_AD_flu1          # This estimates the NEU residual variances
mean_AD_flu2 ~~resNEUvar*mean_AD_flu2          # This estimates the NEU residual variances

#Dynamics

dmean_AD_bl~NEUselfFB*NEUlv_T1         # This estimates the NEU self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)
dmean_AD_flu1~NEUselfFB*NEUlv_T2       # This estimates the NEU self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)

dRAVLT_DELAY_bl~COGselfFB*COGlv_T1         # This estimates the COG self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)
dRAVLT_DELAY_flu1~COGselfFB*COGlv_T2       # This estimates the COG self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)

dmean_AD_bl~COG_to_NEU*COGlv_T1         # This estimates the COG to NEU coupling parameter
dmean_AD_flu1~COG_to_NEU*COGlv_T2       # This estimates the COG to NEU coupling parameter

dRAVLT_DELAY_bl~NEU_to_COG*NEUlv_T1          # This estimates the NEU to COG coupling parameter
dRAVLT_DELAY_flu1~NEU_to_COG*NEUlv_T2        # This estimates the NEU to COG coupling parameter

iCOG=~1*COGlv_T1                   # This defines the COG intercept measurement model
sCOG=~1*dRAVLT_DELAY_bl+1*dRAVLT_DELAY_flu1     # This defines the COG slope measurement model
iCOG~1                             # This estimates the COG intercept intercept (mean)
iCOG~~iCOG                         # This estimates the COG intercept variance
sCOG~1                             # This estimates the COG slope intercept
sCOG~~sCOG                         # This estimates the COG slope variance

iNEU=~1*NEUlv_T1                   # This defines the NEU slope measurement model
sNEU=~1*dmean_AD_bl+1*dmean_AD_flu1      # This defines the NEU slope measurement model
iNEU~1                             # This estimates the NEU intercept intercept (mean)
iNEU~~iNEU                         # This estimates the NEU intercept variance
sNEU~1                             # This estimates the NEU slope intercept
sNEU~~sNEU                         # This estimates the NEU slope variance

iNEU~~sNEU                      # This estimates the iNEU sNEU covariance
iNEU~~sCOG                      # This estimates the iNEU sCOG covariance
iNEU~~iCOG                      # This estimates the iNEU iCOG covariance
iCOG~~sCOG                      # This estimates the iCOG sCOG covariance
iCOG~~sNEU                      # This estimates the iCOG sNEU covariance
sCOG~~sNEU                      # This estimates the sCOG sNEU covariance
'

#fit
fitBDCS <- lavaan(BDCS, data=DF_lcm,
                  estimator='mlr',
                  missing='fiml',
                  group = 'Age_group')

Dear lavaan users,

Please find below a call for articles from the (new) free and
open-access journal 'Quantitative and Computational Methods in
Behavioral Sciences'.

Yves.

--

Dear colleagues,

We are happy to announce that the first issue of "Quantitative and
Computational Methods in Behavioral Sciences" (QCMB) is out
(https://qcmb.psychopen.eu/index.php/qcmb/issue/view/301)! QCMB is a
both-side open access peer-reviewed journal inviting submission of
articles on quantitative methods from all areas of behavioral sciences.

Due to funding and support of the PsychOpen Gold program of the Leibniz
Institute for Psychology, QCMB is fully open access - All articles are
published under creative commons licenses, there are no article fees for
authors, and all articles are accessible free of charge.

QCMB has a fundamental research section, which targets an audience of
quantitative psychologists, mathematicians, and statisticians with an
interest in psychological applications of computational, statistical,
and mathematical models. In this section, we invite articles that
advance fundamental research in the field of quantitative methods.
Articles in this section may very well target only a narrow audience
aiming at a 'deep impact', that is, we hope for articles that do not
necessarily have many readers directly, but enable others to use novel
theoretical results as building blocks for new methods or software.
Complementing this section, QCMB also has a method dissemination
section, in which we invite methodological articles and tutorials that
target a broader audience of social scientists who want to apply modern
statistical and computational methods.

If you are interested in publishing in QCMB, please visit us at

On 2/14/22 16:26, Laura Havers wrote:
> Error in lav_data_cluster_patterns(Y = X[[g]], clus = clus, cluster =

The error message (where 'everything' should be 'every', will fix that)
indicates that each cluster has only 1 observation.

> model_22 <-
>    'p22 =~ p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5 + p6 + p7 + p8 + p9 + p10 + p11 + p12
> + p13 + p14 + p15'
> fit_model_22 <- cfa(model_22, data=data, group = "random", cluster =
> "famID", estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=F, missing = "fiml")
> summary(fit_model_22, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)

> N = 13555, with two family members per family (so two rows /
> participants have the same value for "famID").

What is the "random" variable? I think you need to remove the group =
"random" altogether.

As you seem to have two family members only, you may consider reshaping
your data in 'wide format', so that the variables of the two family
members are in the same row, and the rows become the families.

See: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1689366

This paper is mostly about categorical data, but it works equally well
with continuous data.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: robust covariances from fitted ML model
messages.body_plain:
On 2/14/22 17:04, Jek wrote:
> Is it possible to generate the covariance matrix of the estimates, gamma
> matrix (n times the asymptotic variance matrix of the sample
> statistics), and test statistics from other ML based estimators (e.g.,
> MLR) from an already fitted model with `estimator = “ML”`? Is there a
> helper function within `lavaan` that can accomplish this similar to how
> `sandwich::vcovHC(lm_object)` returns the heteroskedastic-consistent
> covariance matrix of fitted `lm` models?

No. Not out of the box. But you can extract the ingredients (using
lavInspect()) from a fitted lavaan object.
> The solution I have at the moment is to extract the data from the fitted
> `lavaan` object, reconstruct the model from the parameter table, and
> then re-fit the model with a robust ML-based estimator (e.g., MLR). I
> was wondering if there is a less clunky solution which, hopefully, does
> not involve refitting the model.

If you provide the parameter table from the ML-fitted object as input
(the first argument of sem()), and set optim.method = "none", that
should do the trick:

library(lavaan)
example(cfa)

PT <- parameterTable(fit)
fit.mlr <- sem(PT, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, optim.method = "none",
estimator = "MLR", verbose = TRUE)
vcov(fit.mlr)

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: BDCS model with two groups
messages.body_plain:
Everywhere you have a named parameter that you want to vary across groups, add two names.

E.g.

dmean_AD_bl~NEUselfFB*NEUlv_T1         # This estimates the NEU self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)

becomes:

dmean_AD_bl ~ c(NEUselfFB_young, NEUselfFB_old) * NEUlv_T1         # This estimates the NEU self-feedback parameter (equality constrained across timepoints)

In your code it is equality constrained across time point AND group. If you make that change, it's equality constrained across time point, but not across group.

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am conducting a multigroup confirmartory factor analysis using lavaan to test measurement invariance of a 21-items questionnaire across two groups.
Following the procedure illustrated by Svetina et al., 2019 for ordinal responses, I first fitted a configural model, then a thresholds model and compare the two.
When I check the results I get that the two models have the same degrees of freedom and, so, they cannot be compared. Surprisingly, though, the estimated model paramters differ, with the configural model having -obviously- less parameters that the thresholds one.
Even more surprisingly, when I fit the loadings model and compare it to the thresholds one I do get a difference in terms of degrees of freedom. It seems that something is wrong at the configural vs. thresholds models level.
Do you have any idea of why I am encountering this issue and how I can solve it?

Just some details:
-My sample size is N=301, distributed in 196 subs for group 1 and 106 for group 2 (I know it might be small and unbalanced).
-I am testing a bifactor model with a general factor and 3 sub-factors.
-The response scale is 7-point Likert, thus I am treating my variables as ordinal.
-Since some response categories where empty for some items (meaning that in one group none of the participants responded using one of the response category), I collpsed the responses category from 7 to 3.

Here is the R script with the syntax if you want to take a look:

bifactor.model <- '
FattoreG =~ B3 + B4 + B7+ B12 + B19 + B20 + B21 + E5 + E7 + E9 + E11 + C1 + C6 + C8  + C13 + C15 + C25 + C29 + C30 + C34 + C35
Beha  =~  B3 + B4 + B7 + B12 + B19 + B20 + B21
EmoCog =~ E5 + E7 + E9 + E11 + C1 + C6  + C15 + C30
Cog =~   C8 + C13 + C25 + C29 + C34 + C35
'
fit.bifactPON_Region <- cfa(bifactor.model, data = dfPON.region, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,                                                                      orthogonal= T  ,ordered = names(dfPON.region[1:21]))

fitMeasures(fit.bifactPON_Region, fit.measures = c("cfi", "tli", "srmr","rmsea"), output = "matrix")

summary(fit.bifactPON_Region)

# CONFIGURAL MODEL
model.config <-  measEq.syntax(configural.model = bifactor.model,
                               data = dfPON.region,
                               ordered = names(dfPON.region[1:21]),orthogonal=T,
                               parameterization = "delta", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                               ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = "Target_NonTarget",group.equal = "configural")

model.baseline <- as.character(model.config)

fit.model.baseline <- cfa(model.baseline,data = dfPON.region,ordered = names(dfPON.region[1:21]),group = "Target_NonTarget")

fitmeasures(fit.model.baseline, fit.measures = c("chisq", "df", "tli", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr"),
            output  = "matrix")

summary(fit.model.baseline)

# THRESHOLDS MODEL
model.thresholds <-   measEq.syntax(configural.model = bifactor.model,
                                    data = dfPON.region,
                                    ordered = names(dfPON.region[1:21]), orthogonal=T,
                                    parameterization = "delta", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                                    ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                                    group = "Target_NonTarget",group.equal = c("thresholds"))

thresholds <- as.character(model.thresholds)

fit_thr <- cfa(thresholds, data = dfPON.region, ordered = names(dfPON.region[1:21]), group = "Target_NonTarget")

fitmeasures(fit_thr, fit.measures = c("chisq", "df", "tli", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr"),
            output ="matrix")

# COMPARE CONFIGURAL AND THRESHOLDS MODEL
lavTestLRT(fit.model.baseline, fit_thr)

Thank you in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Michael--
Wu and Estabrook (2016) explain what is happening. The ordinal data model includes waves of additional parameters which may be estimated, but these are not all identified--you cannot obtain unique best estimates of them--in the configural model. But if you impose equivalence of thresholds, then some of those other parameters *can* be uniquely estimated, and so, lavaan, while imposing constraints on thresholds, relaxes constraints on other parameters. Wu and Estabrook (2016) rather exhaustively illustrate different paths through the various levels of constraints that may be imposed. In addition, having only 3 response categories also puts your model into a special category regarding identification and DF. I believe there are also some lavaan tutorial resources that describe that specific situation.
Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

As much as I am aware, the null should have more df than the user-specified model... Maybe you can provide more information about that.

Hope it helps,
Jošt

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

a reviewer has asked me whether I can account for measurement error in my DV for a linear mixed regressions (clusters of repeated measures = ID).

My go to solution would be to model my DV as latent construct (4 Items) and use the categorical (experimental conditions/groups) IVs as predictors. Effectively replicating a regression with a better way to measure the DV.
In the initial model, I have opted for effect coding (-1/1) for my IVs.

Now I am wondering, will Lavaan create wrong estimates if I used my experimental conditions as IV that are coded as -1 / 1?

This is what the model looks like

model<-
'DV=~x1+x2+x3+x4

DV~y1+y2+y1:y2+age+gender'

y1: Group a =-1; Group b = +1
y2: Group c =-1; Group d = +1
age: continuous
gender: dummy coded 0/1
clusters of repeated measures = ID
Grouping dataset: Country

sem(model, data = df, estimator="MLR", group = "Country", cluster="ID")

I could not find any explanation about this. Intuitively, I would say it should not matter. However, running the same model with dummy coded variables for y1 and y2 gives me different estimates.
Any help would be appreciated.
